Let me analyze the forecast errors in the teaching examples to identify systematic deviation patterns.

Looking at Example 1 (date=2024-07-08):

Model forecast vs True outcome for the first 10 days:
| Day | Model | True | Difference |
|-----|-------|------|------------|
| 1 | 68.76 | 68.58 | -0.18 |
| 2 | 68.33 | 68.78 | +0.45 |
| 3 | 68.79 | 69.24 | +0.45 |
| 4 | 69.58 | 68.61 | -0.97 |
| 5 | 67.75 | 67.92 | +0.17 |
| 6 | 67.78 | 66.04 | -1.74 |
| 7 | 66.21 | 66.05 | -0.16 |
| 8 | 65.96 | 65.02 | -0.94 |
| 9 | 66.05 | 66.04 | -0.01 |
| 10 | 65.02 | 64.79 | -0.23 |

Let me look at the pattern more carefully. The model seems to be under-forecasting when sentiment is positive and over-forecasting when sentiment is negative.

Looking at Example 1 sentiment history vs errors:
Days 1-5 have mixed sentiment (0.67, 1.00, 0.67, 1.00, 1.00)
- Days 1, 2, 5 are slightly under (errors -0.18, -0.45, +0.17)
- Days 3, 4 are reasonably close (0.45, -0.97)

Let me look at a clearer pattern in Example 2:


I notice a more consistent pattern emerging. When sentiment shifts to positive (0.67, 1.00), the model tends to under-forecast by about 0.3 to 0.5. Negative sentiment ( -0.33) also shows predictable under-forecasting around -0.25 to -0.3. The mean reversion rule becomes evident as prices naturally drift toward the historical mean of 68.80, correcting deviations of more than 1.00 from this baseline.
